1107.title: A hymn in Maru
1107.hook: Maru holds the long Solhe and Kabir's song of the true warrior
1107.howItsDone: Kabir's hymn of the true warrior is sung in kirtan in Raga Maru, and its closing lines are quoted by some Sikhs when speaking of the saint-soldier ideal of the Khalsa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Maru, and your line was courage: without fear, and without hate.

A drum sounds in the sky. A target is struck. A fighter has stepped onto the field, and the poem says: now is the time to fight. That's how a verse begins near the end of Raga Maru, and the voice isn't a general's. It's Kabir, the weaver-poet whose verses the Gurus gathered into the Granth. Maru also holds the long Solhe, great extended hymns of the Gurus. But today, Kabir's battlefield, and the kind of warrior he means.
screen: `A DRUM IN THE SKY.` → `A WEAVER ON THE BATTLEFIELD.` → `KABIR'S WARRIOR.`

segments.voice: Here's Kabir, in plain English, not word for word. The battle drum sounds in the sky; the target is struck. The warrior has entered the field; now is the time to fight. Then the lines at its heart: the true warrior is the one who fights for the sake of the deen, and who, even cut apart piece by piece, never leaves the field. Two things are worth hearing closely. First, the drum in the sky. Some readers hear that sky as the inner sky of the mind, where Kabir's battle is fought: against ego, greed, fear and the rest. The poem sounds like a battlefield and points inward. Second, the word deen. Some translators give it as the poor and helpless, so the true warrior fights for the defenseless. Others give it as faith, or the path of righteousness. Both readings have their commentators, and the hymn bears them both. Either way, he isn't fighting for glory, plunder or a grudge, but for something beyond himself. And what makes him a warrior isn't winning. It's staying. Cut apart, he doesn't leave the field. Some Sikhs connect this verse to the ideal of the saint-soldier, a person of prayer who is also ready to stand up for others. Yesterday's courage was without fear and without hate. Kabir gives it a body and a place to stand: in the field, for the deen, all the way through. That's today's line: the true warrior.
screen: `THE DRUM SOUNDS; THE FIELD IS SET.` · `THE BATTLE IN THE MIND'S SKY.` · `FIGHTING FOR THE HELPLESS.` · `NOT WINNING: STAYING.` · then, large: `THE TRUE WARRIOR.`

segments.voice: Sit with your feet down and your back steady, and notice the first thing that pulls you away: an itch, a thought, a plan for later. Each time the mind leaves, don't fight it angrily; see where it went and come back to the breath, as calmly as a soldier returning to post, leaving and returning without a grudge. If you pray, say Waheguru each time you return; if you don't, simply say back, silently.
A hymn in Maru. Kabir's song of the true warrior, who fights for the deen, the helpless or the right, and never leaves the field. Today's word.
Your line: the true warrior. In Kabir's verse, the warrior is the one who stays. See you tomorrow.

1108.title: Raga Tukhari
1108.hook: a raga of cold months and deep feeling
1108.howItsDone: Shabads from the Tukhari section, including Guru Nanak's poem of the months, are sung in Raga Tukhari in kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Maru, and your line was the true warrior: the one who stays on the field.

Frost on a windshield at six in the morning. Breath you can see. A field gone stiff and white, every blade of grass holding still. Cold has its own quiet, and it can make a person feel very far from whoever they love. After the drums of Maru, the Guru Granth Sahib turns to a raga this path hears as one of cold months and deep feeling: Tukhari.
screen: `FROST ON THE WINDSHIELD.` → `AFTER THE DRUMS, THE COLD.` → `RAGA TUKHARI.`

segments.voice: Tukhari holds long, flowing songs of the Gurus, and their mood is longing: a soul like a bride waiting for her Beloved, the Creator, and feeling the distance. To hear that mood at its coldest, go to one verse in Guru Nanak's poem of the months, which opens in full tomorrow. It's the verse for Poh, a winter month. In plain English, not word for word: in Poh the frost falls, and the sap dries up in the forest and the grass. The bride asks, in effect, why haven't you come? Listen to the picture. Not a storm. Frost. Everything alive pulls its sap inward and goes still. That's the winter feeling of this raga: not loud grief, but a quiet ache, the kind that settles in when someone you love is far away. One small detail: the word in that verse for frost is tukhar, very close to the raga's own name. Whether or not the two are related, they keep each other company on the page. And notice what the verse does with the cold. It doesn't pretend it's warm. It names the frost and the dryness, then turns the whole feeling toward the One it longs for. In this poem, longing isn't a failure of faith. It's a form of love. A raga that sings winter honestly takes missing someone seriously. That's today's line: winter feeling.
screen: `A BRIDE, WAITING FOR THE BELOVED.` · `IN POH THE FROST FALLS.` · `THE SAP DRAWS INWARD.` · `LONGING IS A FORM OF LOVE.` · then, large: `WINTER FEELING.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop and your hands rest, the way a winter field goes quiet, and bring to mind someone you miss, far away or gone; don't push the feeling away or stir it up, just let it be present the way frost is on the grass. If you pray, say Waheguru as you breathe out, turning the missing toward the One; if you don't, simply hold that person in mind with care. If missing someone ever grows heavier than you can carry, call or text 988 in the US, or your local emergency number.

Your line: winter feeling. In Guru Nanak's poem, longing is a form of love, not a failure of faith. Until tomorrow.

1109.title: A hymn in Tukhari
1109.hook: Tukhari holds Guru Nanak's own twelve months
1109.howItsDone: Guru Nanak's Barah Maha is sung in Raga Tukhari in kirtan. Guru Arjan's Barah Maha in Raga Majh is read in some gurdwaras at the start of each month of the Indian calendar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Tukhari, and your line was winter feeling: the frost of Poh, and a bride asking why her Beloved hasn't come.

Which month is it where you are? Guru Nanak has a verse for it. A year turns like a wall calendar, each page with its own picture: blossoms, then a hot sun, then rain clouds, then frost. Raga Tukhari holds his Barah Maha, the twelve months, and it walks the whole year, page by page, with a soul longing for its Beloved. Back on day 564 you met Guru Arjan's twelve months in Majh. This one is Guru Nanak's.
screen: `A CALENDAR, PAGE BY PAGE.` → `GURU NANAK'S TWELVE MONTHS.` → `NOW THE WHOLE YEAR.`

segments.voice: The poem opens before any month begins, with a call to listen: our lives are shaped by what we've done, and the soul, like a bride, can't find joy apart from the Beloved. Then the calendar turns. Chet comes first. In plain English, not word for word: Chet is lovely, it's spring, and the bumblebees are beautiful. The forest blooms. And still, the bride says, without the Beloved at home, how can there be peace? A hot month comes, with a scorching sun. The rains come in Savan, and the bride says her mind and body love her Husband Lord. Then the frost of Poh, and on to the end of the year. Every season gets its weather and its longing. Here's the turn at the end. Once the Beloved is met, the poem looks back over everything: the twelve months, the seasons, the days, the hours, the moments, all of them are blessed when the True One comes. The calendar didn't change. The bride did. The Granth's other Barah Maha, Guru Arjan's in Majh, is read in some gurdwaras when a new month begins. But this one is Guru Nanak's own. It doesn't ask for a better season. It asks for the Beloved, and then every season is good. That's today's line: Nanak's months.
screen: `A CALL TO LISTEN.` · `CHET: SPRING AND BUMBLEBEES.` · `HEAT, RAIN, FROST.` · `EVERY MONTH BLESSED WHEN THE ONE COMES.` · then, large: `NANAK'S MONTHS.`

segments.voice: Start with this month: what's the weather outside right now? Feel it for a breath, then let your mind move back a season, and another, the way Guru Nanak's poem moves page by page, finding in each one moment you were glad, however small. If you pray, say Waheguru at each season you pass; if you don't, simply name the moment to yourself.

1110.title: Raga Kedara
1110.howItsDone: Shabads from the Kedara section, including the Bhagats' hymns by Kabir and Ravidas, are sung in Raga Kedara in kirtan, and tradition associates the raga with the evening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Tukhari, and your line was Nanak's months: every season blessed once the Beloved comes.

Evening has its own sound. Dishes clinking. A door closing down the hall. The day's conversations still replaying: who praised you, who didn't, what someone said that stung. Right about then, as the house goes quiet, tradition sets a raga down gently: Kedara, a short section of the Guru Granth Sahib this path calls tender, for the evening. And inside it is a hymn that speaks straight to those replaying conversations.
screen: `DISHES, A DOOR, THE DAY REPLAYING.` → `A TENDER RAGA FOR EVENING.` → `RAGA KEDARA.`

segments.voice: Kedara holds hymns of Guru Ram Das and Guru Arjan, and after them the voices of Bhagats, Kabir and Ravidas. Today, Kabir, in plain English, not word for word: set aside both praise and slander; give up pride and self-conceit. The one who looks on iron and gold alike, Kabir says, is an image of God. Here's how evening can go. The compliments get replayed and polished. The criticism gets replayed and argued with. Both keep the mind awake. Kabir asks for something quieter: let go of both. Not just the insult. The praise too. That's the tender part, and the hard part; setting down a compliment can feel like losing something. One way to read Kabir: praise and blame both tie a person to other people's opinions, and a mind can't rest while it's tied. Iron and gold alike isn't a rule against nice things. It's a picture of a mind that doesn't jump when the world calls it gold, and doesn't sink when the world calls it iron. Evening is a good place for that hymn. The day's verdicts are in, and this is when you can decide not to carry them to bed. Tomorrow, another Bhagat in this raga, at dusk. That's today's line: tender evening.
screen: `GURUS FIRST, THEN KABIR AND RAVIDAS.` · `SET ASIDE PRAISE AND SLANDER.` · `IRON AND GOLD ALIKE.` · `DON'T CARRY THE VERDICTS TO BED.` · then, large: `TENDER EVENING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one piece of praise from this week and one piece of criticism, and if it helps, picture one in each hand, gold and iron, noticing which feels heavier. Then, on an out-breath, set them both down beside you, like two bags at the end of a long walk. If you pray, say Waheguru as you set them down; if you don't, simply let your hands rest open.
Raga Kedara. A short, tender evening raga where Kabir sings: set aside praise and slander, and look on iron and gold alike. Today's word.

1111.title: Listening in Kedara
1111.hook: listen to one Kedara hymn at dusk
1111.howItsDone: Ravidas's hymns are sung in kirtan in their ragas like the Gurus' hymns, and his teaching that birth and caste count for nothing before God is honored in Sikh communities and by the Ravidassia community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Kedara, and your line was tender evening: Kabir setting down praise and blame alike.

Dusk is the hour when titles fade. The office badge comes off. The uniform goes on the hook. In the half-light, a manager and an intern walking home look about the same. This path's practice for Kedara is one hymn at dusk, and there's one made for that hour. It's by Ravidas, the Bhagat who closes the Kedara section, and it's about what's left of a person when the labels come off.
screen: `DUSK: THE TITLES FADE.` → `THE BHAGAT WHO CLOSES KEDARA.` → `RAVIDAS.`

segments.voice: You met Ravidas earlier, singing in Gond. Here he is in Kedara, in plain English, not word for word. A person may perform all the prescribed rituals and come from a high family, but if there's no devotion to the Lord in the heart, and no love for talk of the Lord, that person stands no higher than the one their society looks down on. Then Ravidas turns to his own mind: wake up, careless mind. Look at Valmiki, the poet of the old story, and how high devotion lifted him from a birth others scorned. Listen to the order. First a verdict on others, then a wake-up call to himself. Ravidas doesn't stand outside the problem pointing in; he includes his own careless mind. Then an example, not an argument: Valmiki, one life, lifted. Ravidas takes the scale that ranked people by birth and ritual and sets devotion in its place. Rank by family: gone. Rank by ceremony: gone. What remains is the heart. That's why dusk suits him. In the half-light, labels fade, and what's left of a person is what they love. The Gurus set this hymn in their book, beside their own. Listening at dusk, there's no need to judge anyone, yourself included. Just hear a voice that turns first to its own careless mind, and let the light go. That's today's line: dusk in kedara.

segments.voice: Let your eyes soften as if the light is going, and silently name one label you carry, your job title, a role in your family, a word others use for you, letting it fade on the out-breath, then another, without judging any of them. When they've dimmed, notice what's still here, breath, a body, whatever you love, and rest there. If you pray, say Waheguru softly; if you don't, simply stay with the breath.

1112.title: Raga Bhairao
1112.hook: a serious morning raga that opens with one plain line: nothing happens outside you
1112.howItsDone: In kirtan, ragis sing shabads from the Bhairao section of the Guru Granth Sahib in Raga Bhairao, and tradition associates the raga with the early part of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, listening in Kedara as the light went, and your line was dusk in kedara: devotion counting where birth doesn't.

The alarm goes off, and before your feet find the floor the day already has weight. A hard conversation at ten. A hospital visit after lunch. A letter that can't wait another week. Not every morning is bright and bouncy, and pretending otherwise doesn't help. The Guru Granth Sahib has a raga for mornings like that: Bhairao, sometimes written Bhairo. Tradition gives it a grave, unhurried mood, sung early, when the day is still deciding what it will be.
screen: `THE DAY ALREADY HAS WEIGHT.` → `SOME MORNINGS ARE SERIOUS.` → `RAGA BHAIRAO.`

segments.voice: In the Granth's order, Bhairao comes right after Kedara, yesterday's dusk raga, so the book turns a page from evening to morning. Its pages hold hymns by Gurus and by Bhagats whose words the Gurus set beside their own, Kabir and Namdev among them; one of those is for tomorrow. Today, the door in. The section begins with a hymn of Guru Nanak, and its first line is almost too plain to notice. In paraphrase: nothing happens outside of you. You make it, you watch over it, and you know it. No storm, no miracle. Just a sentence about who holds the day. Now hear it with a serious morning in mind. The hard conversation is still at ten. The line doesn't cancel it. It changes the size of the room it happens in. The conversation, the hospital, the letter, all of it sits inside something larger, made and watched and known. Serious doesn't have to mean gloomy. A serious morning can be an honest one: you see the weight clearly, and you also see you're not the only one holding it. That may be why tradition hears gravity in Bhairao rather than sadness. Teachers describe the moods of ragas in different ways, so hold the mood as tradition, not as a rule written in the Granth. What is written is the line: nothing outside you. That's today's line: serious morning.
screen: `AFTER KEDARA: EVENING TURNS TO MORNING.` · `GURUS AND BHAGATS IN ONE SECTION.` · `NOTHING HAPPENS OUTSIDE OF YOU.` · `SERIOUS CAN MEAN HONEST, NOT GLOOMY.` · then, large: `SERIOUS MORNING.`

segments.voice: If you can, play a shabad sung in Raga Bhairao, or simply sit in the quiet, and silently name the heaviest thing waiting for you today. Don't solve it; lay it in front of you like a letter face up on a table, and let the breath go long and slow around it. If you pray, hold Guru Nanak's opening thought beside it, that nothing happens outside the One; if you don't, simply notice that the thing is there and you are still breathing.
Raga Bhairao. The section that follows Kedara in the Granth, a raga tradition sings early with a grave, steady mood, opening with Guru Nanak's line that nothing happens outside the One. Today's word.
Your line: serious morning. A heavy day can be serious without being the whole sky. More tomorrow.

1113.title: A hymn in Bhairao
1113.hook: Namdev carries a cup of milk to the Lord, and Guru Arjan names the One he serves
1113.howItsDone: Namdev's hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib are sung in kirtan alongside the Gurus' own, and the milk hymn in Bhairao is retold with the story of the boy Namdev making the offering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Bhairao, and your line was serious morning: nothing happens outside the One.

A brown cow, a pail, and someone who has been given a job. He milks the cow, pours the milk into a cup, fills a jug with water, and carries both to the Lord. Then he waits for the Lord to drink. That's the opening of a hymn by Bhagat Namdev, in his own words, in the Bhairao section of the Guru Granth Sahib. You may remember this cup from Namdev's week in year three. Today it gets a second, slower look.
screen: `A BROWN COW AND A CUP.` → `HE CARRIES IT TO THE LORD.` → `AND WAITS.`

segments.voice: Here's the hymn, in paraphrase. Namdev milks the brown cow and brings the milk in a cup, with water in a jug. He sets it before the Lord and pleads: drink this, Lord, and my mind will be at peace. If you don't, my father at home will be angry. Then the turn. A golden cup, filled with nectar, is set before the Lord, and the hymn has God say that this one devotee lives in his heart, and smile on seeing Namdev. The Lord drinks the milk. The devotee goes home, and Namdev has seen the Lord. Tradition fills in the edges: Namdev was a child, and his father, who usually made the daily offering, had asked him to do it. The hymn itself keeps it simple: a cup, a plea, a smile, an empty cup. What stays with people is his directness. He doesn't offer the milk as a ritual to perform and clear away. He offers it as a gift to someone really there, and he means it to be received. The same section holds a hymn of Guru Arjan about serving only the One who protects in the end, which says body and breath belong to the One called both Allah and Ram. Two voices, one point: devotion is offered to someone present. And looking back over this week, from Maru's true warrior through Tukhari's months, Kedara's tender evening and Bhairao's serious morning, each raga has handed over something to carry. Today it's a cup. Your line: the milk offering.
screen: `MILK IN A CUP, WATER IN A JUG.` · `DRINK, AND MY MIND WILL BE AT PEACE.` · `THE LORD SMILES AND DRINKS.` · `OFFERED TO SOMEONE PRESENT.` · then, large: `THE MILK OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary thing you'll give today, a meal you'll cook, a message you'll answer, an hour of work, and hold it the way Namdev holds the cup: not a chore to clear, but something meant to be received. Breathe slowly around it. If you pray, offer it with Waheguru on the breath; if you don't, simply let the giving be wholehearted.
